title: Regular Exercise Erases Half of Muscle Aging's Molecular Signature, Study Finds
excerpt: A multiomics study published in Nature Aging found that physically trained older adults retain youthful gene expression profiles in skeletal muscle, with 50% of age-related molecular differences absent compared to their sedentary peers.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Regular exercise can erase 50% of age-related molecular changes in older adults' muscles.
  • The study utilized multiomics to analyze gene activity, fats, and metabolites in muscle biopsies.
  • Fitter older adults showed stronger immune responses to exercise, indicating better muscle adaptation.
  • The research distinguishes between preventable and unavoidable molecular changes due to aging.

Trained Muscles Look Molecularly Younger

Researchers at Amsterdam UMC and Maastricht University have demonstrated that sustained physical training can erase roughly half the molecular fingerprint of aging in human skeletal muscle. The findings, published on July 3 in Nature Aging, represent one of the most comprehensive multiomics investigations of how exercise reshapes the aging process at a cellular level.

The team, led by Georges E. Janssens and Riekelt H. Houtkooper at Amsterdam UMC's Laboratory of Genetic Metabolic Diseases, performed transcriptomics, lipidomics, and metabolomics on skeletal muscle biopsies from young adults and older adults with varying levels of physical function. Critically, they examined samples both at rest and after an acute bout of submaximal exercise, allowing them to capture not just baseline differences but also how muscles respond to physical stress.

At baseline, older adults exhibited reduced expression of genes tied to cellular respiration and energy metabolism compared to young adults with comparable daily activity levels. But in trained older adults — those who had maintained a regular exercise regimen — 50% of these age-related differences were simply absent. Their molecular profiles more closely resembled those of young participants.

The 'Preventable' Versus 'Unavoidable' Divide

One of the study's most significant contributions is its distinction between age-related molecular changes that respond to exercise and those that do not. The accompanying Nature Aging research briefing described the findings as revealing "distinct transcriptomic patterns of 'preventable' and 'unavoidable' alterations."

The preventable changes — those erased by training — were concentrated in genes governing mitochondrial function, energy metabolism, and cellular respiration, the very pathways that power muscle contraction and endurance. The unavoidable changes persisted regardless of fitness level, pointing to aspects of biological aging that exercise alone cannot override.

This distinction matters for the growing field of longevity medicine, as it helps delineate where lifestyle intervention is most potent and where pharmaceutical or genetic approaches might eventually be needed.

Fitter Bodies Respond Better to Exercise

The study also revealed that a single bout of exercise triggered transcriptional immune and stress responses across all participants, young and old. However, the magnitude of these responses in older adults was positively correlated with their physical fitness — fitter individuals mounted a stronger molecular response to the same exercise challenge.

This finding suggests that regular training does not merely preserve a youthful baseline; it also primes the body to derive greater benefit from each workout. The integrated multiomic analyses further uncovered connections between mitochondrial respiration, lipid metabolism, stress responses, and NAD+ biology — a coenzyme whose decline with age has been linked to metabolic dysfunction and frailty.

"These findings demonstrate that sustained physical training transforms age-related molecular profiles and provide a molecular atlas for study of fitness-dependent aging mechanisms."

— Janssens et al., Nature Aging (2026)

Building on a Decade of Research

The study builds on a series of investigations from the same research group. In 2022, Janssens and colleagues published findings in Nature Aging showing that NAD+ abundance in human muscle is positively associated with healthy aging and muscle function. A 2024 study identified a conserved complex lipid signature — specifically elevated levels of bis(monoacylglycero)phosphates (BMPs) — that marks muscle aging and responds to short-term exercise.

The current study integrates these threads into a unified multiomics framework, analyzing gene expression, lipids, and metabolites from the same muscle samples. This approach allowed the team to map how different molecular layers interact during aging and how exercise disrupts those interactions.

The research was supported by a Longevity Impetus Grant from the Norn Group, the European Union's Horizon Europe program, and the Netherlands Organization for Scientific Research.

What This Means for Everyday Health

For anyone concerned about aging — and for the Indian diaspora, where preventive health awareness has surged in recent years — the study delivers a clear message: sustained physical training has measurable, molecular-level effects on how muscles age. The benefits extend beyond visible strength or endurance gains to fundamental changes in gene expression, metabolism, and cellular resilience.

The research aligns with a broader body of evidence that exercise functions as what some scientists call a "polypill" — a single intervention that simultaneously targets multiple disease pathways. With India's growing fitness culture and the diaspora's increasing focus on longevity and wellness, these findings reinforce that regular physical activity remains the most accessible and evidence-backed tool for healthy aging.

What the study does not answer is what specific exercise regimen produces the greatest molecular benefit, or whether these changes are reversible if training stops. Future research from the Amsterdam UMC group is expected to explore optimal exercise protocols and investigate whether the unavoidable molecular changes can be targeted through other means.
